a: for if we live in him, we will be found
p: The Syriac and the long recension add 'in him'.

readings.w: Lake's text (G L)

readings.plain: for if we live in him, we will be found

readings.w: The Syriac (S) and the long recension (g) (Lake's footnote)

readings.plain: for if we live in him, we will be found in him

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake's Greek. Lake's own English, 'if we live in him we shall be found in him', gives the sense of the longer reading; the words added make plain what 'found' means (compare Philippians 3:9, 'and be found in him').

a: I did not think I should go as far as this
p: Lake: 'The text is here confused and corrupt in all the authorities.' The Greek manuscript hardly makes sense; Lake and Lightfoot mend it differently.

readings.w: Lake's text: the Greek manuscript mended with the Armenian (A) and the long recension (g) in the first half (Lightfoot's apparatus); Lake's 'not' (οὐκ) is not in the Greek manuscript, and he gives no note on it
readings.orig: ἀγαπῶν ὑμᾶς φείδομαι, συντονώτερον δυνάμενος γράφειν ὑπὲρ τούτου. οὐκ εἰς τοῦτο ᾠήθην
readings.en: loving you I spare (you), being able to write more sharply about this; not to this did I think
readings.plain: I did not think I should go as far as this

readings.w: Lightfoot's text (Lake's footnote): he adds οὕτως and the words in brackets, which are his own conjecture 'in accordance with the general sense of A'
readings.orig: ἀγαπῶν ὑμᾶς οὕτως φείδομαι, συντονώτερον δυνάμενος γράφειν ὑπὲρ τούτου· [ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ ἱκανὸν ἑαυτὸν] εἰς τοῦτο ᾠήθην
readings.en: loving you so, I spare (you), being able to write more sharply about this; [but I did not think myself fit] for this
readings.plain: but I did not think myself fit for this

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G), with the Latin (L) following it (Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.orig: ἀγαπῶντας ὡς οὐ φείδομαι ἑαυτὸν πότερον δυνάμενος γράφειν ὑπὲρ τούτου εἰς τοῦτο ᾠήθην
readings.en: loving, as I do not spare myself whether being able to write about this, to this I thought
readings.plain: (no clear sense)

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake. The Armenian has the negative in sense ('but I am not sufficient to command you like an apostle', Lightfoot's Latin of it), and Lake's English ('I did not think myself competent') gives the sense Lightfoot's added words make explicit. Lightfoot says that some words have dropped out, but 'What these were it is impossible to say'.
b: Lightfoot: 'The agreement of A and g establishes one unquestionable emendation; ἑαυτὸν πότερον is a corruption of συντονώτερον' ('more sharply'), and 'The coincidence of the same authorities shows that ἀγαπῶν is correct'. He thinks the archetype of the Greek manuscript and the Latin 'must have been much worn and probably mutilated in this part'.

a: These people weave Jesus Christ in with themselves
t: A corrupt sentence: who mixes what?
p: Lake: 'The text is clearly corrupt.' Lightfoot mends it: 'they even mingle poison with Jesus Christ'.

readings.w: Lake's text, the reading the Syriac (S) and Armenian (A) seem to imply (Lake's footnote)
readings.en: who weave Jesus Christ in with themselves
readings.plain: These people weave Jesus Christ in with themselves

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G) (Lake: 'G(L)'; Lightfoot takes the Latin's 'which also entangles with defiled things' for a further misreading of the same letters)
readings.en: the times weave in Jesus Christ
readings.plain: The times weave in Jesus Christ

readings.w: A quotation in the Rupefucaldine Parallels (Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: and they weave in Jesus Christ
readings.plain: And they weave in Jesus Christ

readings.w: The long recension (g) (Lake's footnote; Lightfoot gives it in full)
readings.orig: καὶ τὸν ἰὸν προσπλέκοντες τῆς πλάνης τῇ γλυκείᾳ προσηγορίᾳ
readings.en: and weaving the poison of error in with the sweet name
readings.plain: These people weave the poison of error in with a sweet name

readings.w: Lightfoot's emendation, which he prints (Lake's footnote); Voss had proposed ἰοῖς ('poisons')
readings.orig: οἳ καὶ ἰῷ παρεμπλέκουσιν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν
readings.en: who even mingle poison with Jesus Christ
readings.plain: These people even mix poison in with Jesus Christ

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake's printed text, though he calls it uncertain. 'The times' makes no sense; Lightfoot's 'poison' is 'a very simple change' in the Greek letters (kaiōi for kairoi, his words) and fits the poison of the next clause. No witness has his words, but he says the long recension's paraphrase 'points to the true reading'.
b: Lightfoot thinks the Syriac and Armenian 'may have had simply οἱ καὶ παρεμπλέκουσιν and supplied the semetipsos ("themselves") to make sense'. His hoi is the relative 'who', with the heretics understood from 'heresy' in 6:1 (he compares Thucydides 6.80). Read with Lake, the false teachers mix Christ's name into their own teaching to win trust; read with Lightfoot, they lace Christ with poison.

p: The Latin has 'evil pleasure'; the Syriac and Armenian lack 'evil'; the Greek manuscript reads 'and therein is death'.

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake, who prints the Latin's reading. Lightfoot calls the Greek manuscript's 'and therein is death' 'tempting', but says the parallel in Ignatius to the Philadelphians 2:2, where false teachers take captives with 'evil pleasure' (hēdonē kakē), 'is decisive in favour of κακῇ', which 'is also supported by the great preponderance of authorities'.

a: In the same way his Father will also raise us
p: The Greek is awkward; the Syriac and Armenian may have read it more smoothly.

readings.w: Lake's text (G; the Latin qui et secundum similitudinem agrees)

readings.en: as also in the likeness he will so raise us
readings.plain: Just so, in the same likeness, his Father will also raise us

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake. The meaning is the same in both: the Father who raised Jesus will raise believers in the same way. Lake's 'perhaps imply' is a guess about what lay behind the translations, not a Greek reading.
b: Paul uses 'likeness' (homoiōma) of being united with Christ 'in a death like his' and his resurrection (Romans 6:5).

Lightfoot calls περίκειμαι 'obviously corrupt' and knows 'no better emendation' than Bunsen's, 'corresponding to the Latin qua conor potiri', 'but I am not quite satisfied with it'; he says the common text 'might mean "to obtain the lot with which I am invested" ... but this is hardly sense.'

The manuscript's 'you purify' does not fit 'of you' (hymōn) or the parallel in Ignatius to the Ephesians 8:1, 'I give myself as an offering for you', where Lightfoot explains the verb as 'I make myself a ἅγνισμα, a piacular offering'. Lake prints the third person without a footnote.

a: it has peace in flesh and spirit through the suffering of Jesus Christ
p: The Greek manuscript, the Latin and the Armenian read 'blood'; Lake and Lightfoot print 'spirit' from the long recension.

readings.w: Lake's text; Lightfoot's, from the long recension (g)
readings.orig: ἐν σαρκὶ καὶ πνεύματι τῷ πάθει Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
readings.en: in flesh and spirit by the suffering of Jesus Christ
readings.plain: it has peace in flesh and spirit through the suffering of Jesus Christ

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G), the Latin (L) and the Armenian (A) (Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.orig: ἐν σαρκὶ καὶ αἵματι τῷ πάθει Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
readings.en: in flesh and blood by the suffering of Jesus Christ
readings.plain: it has peace in flesh and blood through the suffering of Jesus Christ

readings.w: The Armenian (A) also lacks 'by the suffering' (Lightfoot's apparatus); his alternative mending
readings.orig: ἐν σαρκὶ καὶ αἵματι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
readings.en: in the flesh and blood of Jesus Christ
readings.plain: it has peace in the flesh and blood of Jesus Christ

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake. Lightfoot: 'The existing Greek text ἐν σαρκὶ καὶ αἵματι τῷ πάθει Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ can hardly stand; and I have thought it best to adopt from the interpolator's text πνεύματι'; 'flesh and spirit' is Ignatius's usual pair (Ignatius to the Magnesians 1:2). 'The alternative would be to omit τῷ πάθει, as a gloss', which the Armenian supports; then the words would be aimed at the teaching that Christ only seemed to have a body.
b: Lake prints 'spirit' with no footnote. Roberts and Donaldson's English ('flesh, and blood, and passion') follows the manuscript's 'blood'. Lightfoot notes 'the same confusion of πνεύματι and αἵματι in the authorities' at Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3.

a: in him I saw your whole congregation
p: The Greek manuscript has a middle form of the verb; the long recension has the plain active.

readings.w: Lake's text (G)
readings.orig: ὥστε με τὸ πᾶν πλῆθος ὑμῶν ἐν αὐτῷ θεωρεῖσθαι
readings.en: so that I beheld your whole congregation in him
readings.plain: in him I saw your whole congregation

readings.w: The long recension (g), printed by Lightfoot; the Latin and Armenian also have 'see' (Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.orig: ὥστε με τὸ πᾶν πλῆθος ὑμῶν ἐν αὐτῷ θεωρῆσαι
readings.en: so that I saw your whole congregation in him
readings.plain: in him I saw your whole congregation

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake's text with Lake's own English, 'that I saw your whole congregation in his person': with 'me' as its subject, the middle verb can only mean 'behold'. Lightfoot prefers the active: 'There seems to be no good authority for the middle θεωρεῖσθαι, though it appears in some corrupt texts of classical authors.' The two readings differ in form, not in what Ignatius says.
